The question is when will the global slowdown stabilise? With industrial activity falling across much of Europe, the continent is increasingly reliant on Germany to prevent a sharp contraction. But exports– Germany’s growth driver – are weakening, making a fall in German industry increasingly likely. . A full recovery in European industry depends on significant structural reform across southern Europe to help improve competiveness. Irrespective of the pace of reform, it will be a long time coming. Across the Atlantic, robust growth in US industry through 2011 has ground to a halt in 2012. Domestic demand growth has been tepid at best, as unemployment remains elevated. The recently-announced QE3 may is likely to support US economic growth in the short term, but the impact of this on US industry is likely to be minimal. US industrial growth will be weak in 2013. Turning to the developing world, industrial growth has slowed under the weight of European recession and domestic policy tightening in 2011. Demand for developing economy exports is lacking and the economic slowdown engineered by policymakers through 2011 could turn into a hard landing for those economies dependent upon trade. However, policies in many developing economies, China included, are becoming more supportive of growth. The lagged effect of policy support through 2012 and further stimulus – including infrastructure plans announced in China – will help drive a rebound in developing world industry as we move into 2013. Wood Mackenzie forecasts global industrial production growth to accelerate from 3.3% this year to 4.3% next year. ### **Global growth in industry to be driven by non-OECD economies** 12

## **USA** After experiencing robust growth in 2011, US industrial production growth has lost momentum. Output in August was up by a mere 0.2% from January’s level, up by just 2.8% from a year earlier. The relatively strong growth that US industry enjoyed up until Q2 was largely due to the strength of the capital goods sector, and especially autos. Through much of 2011 and into early 2012, firms invested heavily in capital goods (equipment and software in particular) to take advantage of tax breaks and make their processes more efficient. This assisted recovery in durable goods production but has since fallen away as a driver of industrial production as business investment growth decelerates. Industrial production has also benefited from a surge in auto production, up by 25% year on year in the first 8 months of 2012, as domestic vehicle demand accelerated. But there are also question marks about the sustainability of this driver, as much of the increase in vehicle sales appears to have been met by unsustainable borrowin

g or by households dipping into savings. We expect US GDP and private consumption to expand only modestly in the coming few quarters, constraining industry as we move into 2013. Wood Mackenzie forecasts US IP to expand by 3.9% in 2012 and 1.7% in 2013 respectively. 

We have made no changes to our medium- to long-term outlook for US industrial production since our last update, but there is potential upside stemming from developments in the energy sector. US gas and oil production are expanding,

Consequently, some energy intensive industries, such as petrochemicals and DRI (steel), are likely to expand production as we look into the medium-term (2016 and beyond). While the direct impact of these industries may not be that large, the knock-on effects on related industries may be beneficial to total industrial production growth, especially in the latter half of this decade.

## **Japan** 

Japanese industrial activity enjoyed a bounce in production in early 2012, as output recovered from supply-chain disruptions following the flooding in Thailand in late 2011. But the country has been unable to maintain the momentum through the summer – indeed output contracted almost 4% from May to July. The weakness in industry is predominantly due to poor export demand for Japanese goods, as recession in Europe and slower growth in Asia has impacted Japanese electronics exports in particular. However, other factors have also contributed. Firstly, domestic demand has contracted, following stimulus-aided boost in the first quarter. Secondly and perhaps more importantly, appreciation of the yen resumed in Q2 and has continued through Q3, eroding away the competitiveness and profitability of Japanese manufacturers.  We forecast growth in industrial production of 3.0% for 2012, owing to the base effect of extremely weak output following the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami. But given the recent slump in production and the on-going weakness in the global economy, our current forecast of 3.1% growth in 2013 is looking increasingly optimistic. 

Our view on Japanese growth over the long-term remains unchanged but downside risks remain. The steady decline in Japan’s working age population (which began in 1997 and is gathering momentum) is a key factor pushing Japan’s overall IP growth down to 1% per annum by 2020. Recent developments have the potential to push growth down further. Japan’s high value-add manufacturing has been under threat for some time from growth in high-tech industrial economies such as South Korea and Singapore, where costs are lower and an increasingly skilled labour force available. Bu the decision to phase out nuclear power generation in the coming decades may push up power prices for Japanese industry. This, together with the strong yen, pr

ovide a potential reason firms to reassess their investment plans and step up the pace of industrial off-shoring. 

## **South Korea** 

After a couple of years of rapid expansion, growth in Korea’s industrial sector ground to a halt during 2011. Signs emerged in early 2012 that output had turned a corner and was growing once again but hopes were premature. Output in July was 3% below its peak in February, and was flat in terms of annual growth. Korean industry is very much dependent on exports, and demand from the key export markets of China and Europe has disappointed. While prospects for a shortterm recovery in European demand are limited, we do expect to see improving export demand from other markets (most notably China) toward year-end and into 2013. Wood Mackenzie expects industrial growth to slow to 3.5% this year from 6.9% in 2011. In 2013, IP growth is forecast to accelerate to 4.9% but this is predicated on a pick-up in Chinese demand that has yet to materialise. Through the rest of the decade, growth in Korean industry is forecast to remain robust, albeit growing at a slower pace than that experienced over the past 30 years.  This is due to a declining working age population and slower productivity gains.  Growth is expected to then gradually slow to 3.5% by the end of the forecast period in 2030.

## **Europe** 

The periphery of Europe is experiencing sharp contraction in economic activity as austerity bites and restructuring takes time.  Arguably, the problems facing Europe’s industrial sector are even more acute than those facing the wider economy. Industrial production in the EU27 fell 1.8% in July (year on year), and the level of activity remains extremely low by historical standards. Wood Mackenzie’s latest forecast expects IP in Europe to shrink by 1.4% this year before growing 1.7% in 2013. 

There are concerns that the loss of IP in much of Europe will be permanent. Put simply, a level of capacity has been destroyed. If this is true then a pickup in the European economy may not foster a full industrial recovery in some countries. However, there are reasons to be more positive about the European outlook. In September, the European Central Bank’s (ECB) announcement of a new bond purchase scheme stabilised the euro crisis for now. Furthermore peripheral economies are regaining competitiveness in terms of falling unit labour costs. Nominal unit labour costs have fallen by ~16% in Ireland, ~13% in Greece, ~6% in Spain, and ~5% in Portugal from their 2008/ 2009 highs. 

Most economies in Europe fall into one of three categories in terms of IP; (i) IP remains depressed and some of this loss is permanent; (ii) IP almost recovered to pre-crisis levels but has since gone back into contraction; or (iii) IP has recovered but is growing slower than pre-crisis rates. 

Many of the countries in the southern periphery of Europe, including Spain an

d Italy, are in that first category. They are struggling to recover industrial activity lost during the collapse of 2008/09. In fact, Spanish industrial activity continues to contract. IP is now 28% below the June 2007 peak – primarily due to the collapse in the construction industry which decimated demand for associated capital goods. The construction industry remains weak. Housing starts fell 27% in Q1 2012 compared to the same quarter in 2011. And there is no sign of a pickup as the property boom that peaked in 2006 has left Spain with a significant oversupply of property.  In Italy the situation is similar, industrial output is currently in decline and remains 24% below the April 2008 peak – although construction has been less of a factor. Of particular concern is the decline in output relative to capacity. Italian capacity utilisation is 9% below the pre-crisis level. This suggests that significant manufacturing capacity has been lost in Italy as firms have gone out of business or have reduced the scale of their operations. The implication is that even when Europe’s economy recovers and demand improves, industry cannot recover to the pre-crisis level of output without investing in new industrial capacity. Adding new industrial capacity is not a quick process. 

Core European economies have generally have outperformed their southern counterparts, recovering close to pre-crisis levels. However, industrial output has started to contract once again due to recession across Europe.  Germany’s highly flexible and competitive manufacturing sector was able to respond quickly to robust domestic and emerging market demand for its exports – and this led to a swift recovery in industrial production. But, output has since plateaued and survey data for Germany’s new export orders of manufactured goods suggests a sharp contraction in activity. We expect IP to contract 1.2% this year in Germany. Belgium managed to recover to pre-crisis levels in mid-2011 but has since gone back into contraction. Industrial output slipped back in 2012, and in June 2012 is was 9% below its July 2008 peak. Having produced close to peak levels, there is little to suggest that these core countries have suffered any permanent loss in production. Therefore, when demand begins to pick up we would expect them to fully recover. France and the UK might be the exceptions however. Industrial output is languishing 14% below the pre-crisis peak in France while capacity utilisation in manufacturing is only 8% off its peak – bearing more resemblance to the periphery. 

Among the best performing nations are emerging eastern European economies, albeit at lower annual growth rates than before the crisis.  Having made a full recovery in 2010, industrial activity in Poland is now 10% higher than the previous peak in February 2008. Poland’s IP was buoyed by spillover effects from infrastructure construction associated with hosting the UEFA Football Championships in the summer of 2012. But, the ext

ernal environment is taking its toll with IP growth stagnating so far this year. We expect industrial output growth to accelerate in Poland to 3.5%. 

Wood Mackenzie’s short to medium term outlook for European industrial output is modest. While recent ECB action has helped to stabilise the euro crisis, it is not a resolution in itself. There is no quick fix. Consolidating sovereign debt and improving competitiveness will take time – probably a decade. Furthermore, things are likely to get worse before they get better as unemployment is yet to peak in much of the periphery. Industrial output will suffer in the short-term due to continued fiscal consolidation and reduced demand for European exports by Asian economies. Protracted restructuring in Europe will weigh on economic growth and industrial production over the medium term outlook. 

Significant downside risks remain in the short term. Parliamentary elections are planned in  Italy (spring 2013) and Germany (autumn 2013) and the victors must remain supportive of the euro project for it to succeed into the long term. Political change in Europe could result in some sort of unwinding of the monetary union. Any sort of Eurozone breakup would result in severe contraction in economic activity and industrial production across Europe and an even more prolonged recovery to pre-crisis levels of output. 

Europe’s long term growth prospects are marginally more positive than in the previous update. Labour market reform in Spain and Italy supports a more robust outlook. More flexible labour markets and increased participation rates are expected to reduce  costs within industry and increase potential output. IP growth for the whole of Europe is forecast to

average 1.4% per annum over the period 2020-30. A divergence between growth in the developed western European nations and the emerging central and eastern nations will be evident. Western European countries will be constrained by significant demographic factors – ageing populations and in some instances shrinking working age population. Germany and Italy alone will see their working age populations shrink by around a total of 11 million people over the next two decades (3m in Italy and 8m in Germany). In order to maintain output at close to current levels, labour force participation rates and productivity will need to increase to offset this demographic change. In emerging nations, growth will be higher since the potential for productivity gains is greater and they will transition to higher value added industries through time.

## **China** 

China’s economy is slowing admittedly more than we expected, but fears of a hard landing are overblown in our view. Industrial production growth has slowed from 12.8% year on year in December 2011 to 8.9% in August. There are two key drivers of t

his slow down. Firstly, export growth has fallen sharply this year due to the weakness in overseas demand, primarily European demand. Exports to Europe fell by 15% and 13% year on year in July and August respectively. The second drag on growth is China’s construction sector, with commercial house building experiencing a downturn in 2012. This has knock-on implications for many industries, from steel to household goods. On top of this, policy response has been somewhat muted. Monetary easing has been modest and we have not seen a surge in stimulus-driven investment as in 2008/9. 

While demand for China’s exports from Europe in particular is likely to remain weak into 2013, it is still a question of when not if output growth picks up. Government policies are gradually becoming more supportive of growth and we could see further measures announced following the once-in-a-decade transition in China’s leadership this autumn. The new leaders will certainly want to establish themselves with pro-growth policies. Perhaps more importantly, house prices in the majority of China’s largest cities are also rising once again, and residential construction starts increased by 5% year on year in August – the first annual increase since November of last year. We expect to see an improvement in China’s construction sector through the end of 2012 and into 2013 and this will provide a sizeable boost for industry. However, downside risks remain. The build-up of inventories that took place in the first half the year is of concern. Due to destocking, there could be a delay between improving demand in China and improving industrial production. Wood Mackenzie forecasts IP growth of 10.5% in 2012 and 11.3% in 2013. This would make this year the slowest year for IP growth since 2001. 

China’s long-term IP growth is unchanged since our last update. Based on Wood Mackenzie’s assessment of the three primary drivers of potential output to 2030 – growth in productivity, capital stock and the number of workers – we continue to forecast that Chinese industrial growth to gradually decline over the forecast period.  The slowdown is likely to be greater in the next decade, when China’s capital investment needs are not be so great, resulting in weaker investment growth. Wood Mackenzie forecasts Chinese industrial production growth to drop below 10% per annum by 2020, reaching 6.4% in 2030.

## **India** 

India’s industrial sector has performed poorly throughout 2012 as tight monetary policy and a lack of investment has hampered activity. Through the first seven months of 2012, industrial output expanded just 0.2% from the same period a year earlier. The problems facing the Indian economy are numerous but many relate to the lack of investment. Capital goods production, which ties in strongly with investmen

t demand, fell by 5% year on year in July. Unfortunately investment growth in India does not look set to return anytime soon. Business investment is deterred by extremely high interest rates (currently 8% for the benchmark rate) and elevated inflation means interest rates are unlikely to decrease. In addition, investment is hampered by red tape and bureaucratic obstacles, and the current political deadlock means that necessary investment reforms are unlikely before the 2014 general election. Wood Mackenzie forecasts industrial production growth of just 1.8% in 2012, well below the average of growth in the preceding decade of 7.7%. However, we expect annual growth to accelerate in 2013 to 5.5% as reduced inflation allows monetary easing and consumer demand growth accelerates – but weak investment will continue to be a drag on growth. 

Because of the long-term nature of barriers to investment, Wood Mackenzie’s medium to long-term growth projections have been downgraded. The pace of industrial growth is forecast to accelerate slightly in the medium term, peaking at 6.6% in 2015 before decelerating to a little over 6% per annum through the forecast period to 2030. The cumulative effect of this downgrade means that India’s industrial output will be 10% lower in 2030 than it was in our previous forecast. 

## **Brazil** 

In 2011 industrial growth in Brazil slowed to 0.3% from 10.6% the previous year. Unfortunately for Brazil, manufacturing has continued to slump into 2012, weighed down by high labour costs, a strong currency, falling investment and a sharp contraction in Brazil’s auto industry in the first half the year. During the first 7 months of 2012, IP has fallen by 4.1% from a year earlier. However, industry is expected to recover somewhat throughout the remainder of the year – tax breaks introduced in June have resulted in a surge in domestic vehicle sales, and the government has introduced a raft of measures to boost manufacturing competiveness. Labour costs will be cut by reducing payroll taxes, electricity tariffs for industry will fall by 28%, and infrastructure bottlenecks are being addressed. As a result of these measures, we expect to see industrial growth return in 2013. Wood Mackenzie forecasts IP to contract by 3.3% this year, but grow by 2.2% next year. 

There is no change to Brazil’s medium- to long-term growth prospects. Brazil’s industrial production growth potential is robust but growth potential remains contingent on the effectiveness of policies to promote productivity growth and provide employment for a growing working age-population. Large-scale investment in infrastructure will also be essential for the economy to realise its potential. Research and development and related investment in the oil and gas sector will support growth going forward and Wood Mackenzie forecast annual IP growth to trend to just over 3% though the medium-to long-term.

Europe is falling back into recession, while the US economy continues to grow (albeit slowly). Europe’s construction sector is also contracting, as the euro crisis continues to deter households and businesses from building. In the US, the housing market is now recovering and looks set to strengthen in the coming years (from a low base). After a promising start to the year – driven by the reconstruction effort following last year’s natural disasters, both the Japanese economy and its construction sector are struggling. In the emerging markets, economic growth has slowed in 2012. But some economies, notably India and Brazil, are also weighed down by domestic problems. The lack of investment in both these countries is feeding through into weakening construction activity this year. However, prospects do seem to be improving for 2013. ## **USA** 2012 is set to be the first year of growth fo

r US construction since 2005. Since 2005, the sector has shrunk 6 consecutive years, taking total construction investment back to levels not seen since the early 1990s. From peak to trough, total construction contracted by 37%, with the residential side of the market accounting for over 90% of the contraction. Indeed, non-residential construction only started to decline in late 2008 as the financial crisis intensified. The extent of the collapse in the US housing market is illustrated by the fall in the residential share of total construction – from 57% in 2005 to 38% in 2011. ### **US real construction investment** 1,600

The US housing market has turned the corner, with robust growth so far in 2012. The rate of new house building is up by 19% from 2011 and permits for new homes reached a 4-year high in July. Recovery in US housing has always been a matter of when, not if. The level of house building activity in the past few years has been far below what is necessary to keep pace with a population rising by 3 million people per annum. In many parts of the country, there is no longer an excess supply of properties following the collapse of the housing bubble, and prices are rising once more. We expect to see robust growth in US housing to continue into the medium term and forecast growth in residential construction investment of 10%+ per annum in 2012-14. A cautionary note however; over the past few years there have been signs of recovery in US housing that did not last, nipped in the bud by faltering economic growth. The non-residential side of US construction is also growing, but not as fast as in the housing market. Non-housing construction expanded at an annual rate of 5.1% in the first half of 2012; a slightly lagged response to strong business investment in late 2011. We are sceptical that such growth can be maintained in the second half of this year as business investment growth has slowed. Indeed, non-residential construction will likely dip before resuming growth next year. Wood Mackenzie forecasts non-residential construction investment will grow by 2.7% in 2012 and 2.9% in 2013. ## **Eurozone** The Eurozone construction sector has contracted each year for the past 4 years. The trend is unlikely to change in 2012 as falling economic activity and the euro debt crisis impact on residential and non-residential construction alike. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2012 Page 8 of 11 Economic Outlook Unsurprisingly, the downturn continues to be most severe in Europe’s periphery, notably Spain and Italy. German construction investment is likely to be flat in 2012. Although recent actions by the European Central Bank have st

abilised the euro debt crisis, falling GDP and rising unemployment will drag on both non-residential and residential construction as we head into 2013. We forecast total Eurozone construction investment to fall by a further 1.6% and 0.5% in 2012 and 2013 respectively. This would take activity to a level 18% below where it was in 2007. The pace of recovery in subsequent years is likely to be mixed. Although we expect the Eurozone as a whole to return to growth in 2014, peripheral economies such as Italy and Spain will likely not see recovery begin before 2015. Even then, the pace of recovery will be very slow and we do not expect to see Eurozone construction investment returning to the peak of 2007 until well into the next decade. For much of this decade activity will be weighed down anaemic economic growth, and then an aging demographic in key economies such as Germany will reduce the need for new homes. ### **Index of construction investment in Europe** 130

## **Japan** Japan’s construction sector has been in (near continuous) decline for twenty years as deflation, demographic shifts and previous overinvestment have resulted in oversupply in both the residential and non-residential sectors. Growth returned in 2011 however, largely due to the recovery efforts following the 3-11 disaster, but that recovery appears to be faltering in 2012. Residential and non-residential construction investment grew by 1.4% and 2.6% respectively in the first half of 2012, well below our expectations at the start of the year. Although robust growth will continue in the northern prefectures most impacted by last year’s disasters, it is hard to see where the drivers of construction growth can come from for the rest of the country given the current economic weakness. Wood Mackenzie forecasts total Japanese construction investment to expand by 2.7% in 2012 and 1.9% in 2013. Despite the projected gains in construction investment over the short term, it is important to highlight the continued presence of underlying structural drivers that led to the past twenty year decline. During its boom years up until the late 1980s, Japan invested heavily, perhaps too heavily, in capital. The country was left with a ‘capital to GDP’ ratio well above any other developed economy, and this is still the case. As such, the need for further investment in real estate is limited. In addition, Japan faces large falls in its population over the coming decades that will reduce housing needs. For these reasons, the next few years are just a positive blip in the long-term trend of falling construction activity in Japan. ## **South Korea** South Korea’s residential construction sector experienced a 35% drop in housing investment in a six-year period from 2005 to 2011, as changes in government policy led to fewer public construction projects and house prices tumbled. The market is recovering through 2012, with improved house-prices leading to a flurry of new housing orders – permits authorized for new homes rose 10% year on year through H1. We do not expect such a pace of growth to be maintained through H2, as the most recent data suggests that housing sales have been sliding in Q3. Nevertheless, Wood Mackenzie forecasts residential construction investment to expand by 5% in 2012. Coupled with on-going steady growth in the non-residential sector, this will result in total construction growth this year of 3.2% in 2012 and 3.3% in 2013. We expect to see a modest acceleration in the medium term, but this will be difficult to sustain in the long term given Korea’s lack of population growth. ### **Total construction growth** 30%

Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - September 2012 Page 10 of 11 Economic Outlook ## **India** The boom enjoyed by India’s construction sector in recent years has come to an abrupt halt. A rapidly growing middleclass demanding more homes, firms expanding industrial capacity, and growing infrastructure investment resulted in construction activity increasing 61% between 2005 and 2011. But rapid monetary tightening in 2010 and 2011, not to mention excessive red tape and regulation, has severely dampened investment and disrupted economic growth in India. Wood Mackenzie forecasts total construction investment in India to fall by 2% in 2012, the first such fall in a decade. We expect growth to return in subsequent years as reduced inflationary pressures allow monetary policy to ease and policy reform facilitates investment. Strong growth through the long-term will be supported by India’s rapidly rising demand for modern housing, infrastructure, retail and office space, although bureaucratic red-tape remains a significant downside risk to the outlook. ## **Brazil** Expansion in Brazil’s construction activity slowed to 4.1% in 2011, down from 12% in 2010. The slowdown was the result of rising credit costs as monetary policy tightened through the first half of the year. Construction labour costs have also increased sha

rply, owing to a shortage of qualified workers required for modern construction processes. While monetary policy has since eased, the problems for the construction sector continue and investment growth is lacking. Over the first 7 months of 2012, construction activity grew by just 1.7% year on year. We do expect to see things improve through the second half of this year and into 2013 however, as government policies provide a boost to investment and industry alike. Infrastructure investment plans are being accelerated, and tax cuts on building materials should help bring down costs. In addition, Brazil continues to build increasing numbers of social houses under the _My House, My_ Life scheme.
